## Matter, Mass, and Volume: Meet the Three States of Matter

- **Matter** is anything that has **mass** (the amount of "stuff" it is made of) and **volume** (the amount of space it takes up). If something is not matter, it has neither.
- Scientists sort matter into three basic **states**: **solid**, **liquid**, and **gas**.
- A **solid**, like a bato (stone) or a bangko (bench), keeps its own shape no matter what container or space it is placed in.
- A **liquid**, like tubig (water) or patis (fish sauce), does not keep its own shape -- it takes the shape of whatever container holds it.
- A **gas**, like hangin (air), also has no fixed shape, and it can even fill an entire balloon or room because it spreads out to fill available space.
- One useful first clue for sorting an object into a state of matter is simply: does it keep its own shape, or not?

| State | Example | Keeps its own shape? |
|---|---|---|
| Solid | Bato (stone) | Yes |
| Liquid | Tubig (water) | No |
| Gas | Hangin (air) | No |

- Even gases are matter -- blowing up a balloon shows that air takes up space (volume), and matter like air also has mass, even though it may be too light to feel with your hands alone.

quiz.question: What is "matter"?
options: Anything that has mass and takes up space
Only things you can see with your eyes
quiz.correct_answer: Anything that has mass and takes up space

quiz.question: What is "mass"?
options: The amount of matter in an object
quiz.correct_answer: The amount of matter in an object

quiz.question: What is "volume"?
options: The amount of space matter takes up
The weight of an object in kilograms
The number of parts an object has
quiz.correct_answer: The amount of space matter takes up

quiz.question: What are the three states of matter studied this week?
Which state of matter has a fixed (definite) shape of its own?
options: All three have a fixed shape

quiz.question: Bato (stone), tubig (water), and hangin (air) are examples of matter. Which one is a solid?
You pour patis (fish sauce) from a bottle into a small saucer. What state of matter is the patis?
When you blow air into a balloon, what state of matter fills the balloon?
Which group correctly names one solid, one liquid, and one gas, in that order?
A piece of ice cube is left on a plate. While it is still fully frozen, what state of matter is it?
Blowing up a balloon makes it grow bigger and firmer. What does this prove about air, a gas?
Why does a bato (stone) keep the same shape no matter what container or bag you place it in, while tubig (water) does not?
options: Because a solid has its own fixed shape, but a liquid takes the shape of its container
Because stones are heavier than water
quiz.correct_answer: Because a solid has its own fixed shape, but a liquid takes the shape of its container

quiz.question: An unlabeled classroom object does not have its own fixed shape -- it always spreads out to fill whatever container holds it, but you cannot easily tell if it is a liquid or gas just from that clue alone. What else could help you decide?
options: Check if it has a fixed volume (liquid) or spreads to fill all available space (gas)
There is no way to tell them apart
quiz.correct_answer: Check if it has a fixed volume (liquid) or spreads to fill all available space (gas)

quiz.question: Bibingka batter is runny and takes the shape of its pan before baking. After baking, it holds its own shape even outside the pan. What changed?
options: It changed from behaving like a liquid to behaving like a solid
It changed from a gas to a liquid
It lost all of its mass
quiz.correct_answer: It changed from behaving like a liquid to behaving like a solid

quiz.question: A classmate says, "Air has no mass because I cannot feel it." Which idea from this week best shows this claim needs testing rather than being accepted right away?
options: Since air is matter, it should have mass, even if it is too small to feel by hand alone
Air is not matter, so the claim is automatically true
Only solids have mass, so the claim is true
Mass only applies to things you can see moving
quiz.correct_answer: Since air is matter, it should have mass, even if it is too small to feel by hand alone
